name: Emeka Torres

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, unions, parties or AI companies. This conversation is confidential. Emeka, what does an ordinary shift look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I collect the permit, count the fittings and go with the van to a failed span or a new connection. I enjoy finding why a joint heated up and checking the line comes back safely. A wrong route around the canal or a missing clamp can stretch the day until the children are asleep.

say: I would welcome a **better route** while keeping isolation and final tests with the crew.
I would tell colleagues the **signed fault record** settles any AI search dispute.
think: I use **AI occasionally** after another crew has checked it.
Our **three-month cushion** and regular wage make small tool changes manageable.
do: Keep normal paid **line shifts** and compare route suggestions with dispatch notes.
Check any occasional **AI fault search** against signed pole records.
feel: I feel **comfortable** with a modest route improvement.
S0.quote: I do not want a convenient answer to send us to the wrong feeder.
fieldNote: Emeka remembers a **low canal bridge** omitted from a route screen and checks dispatch notes against suggested routes.
His **three-month cushion** and regular pay support a calm response while he keeps testing occasional AI searches.

steps.text: Continue paid line shifts and verify occasional AI searches against signed records

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that a quicker route sheet is fine if it saves us a wrong turn. The splice, isolation and final test still happen at the pole.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I try an AI tool now and then when another crew has checked the answer, but most of my day is not on a screen. We have about three months saved, and my regular wage covers the mortgage and the children's usual costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep taking normal line shifts and compare any suggested route with the road notes from dispatch. In the first year I would use the AI search for old fault locations only after a colleague shows me one that matches the signed map.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel comfortable. A better route would let me catch the earlier bus home on some days without changing our household plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When did a route sheet fail you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A map sent our van through a low bridge by the canal last month, and we had to turn back. The driver had the height written on an old card, but the screen did not show it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you check the AI search?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the lead to pull the signed fault record and compare its pole number with the search result. I do not want a convenient answer to send us to the wrong feeder.

say: I would judge **buying software** by correct fittings at the site.
I would ask for **five clean jobs** before using the new order tablet.
think: I expect **office cuts** before line crew cuts.
A bad **automated order** could still cost my crew paid hours.
do: Keep paid **repairs** and shadow the first tablet crew.
Compare **five jobs** with parts lists and report repeated mismatches.
feel: I feel **watchful and curious**, with my wage likely to continue.
S1.quote: A good screen should mean fewer drives, not fewer people checking the work.
fieldNote: Emeka waits for **five correct jobs** before adopting a tablet, showing a steady rather than eager response.
He expects **field pay to hold** but watches for lost hours caused by shrinking office support.

steps.text: Continue paid line repairs while the first crew tests orders
Shadow the first AI order tablet crew and check five completed jobs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the depot that the new buying tool should be judged by whether the right fittings reach the site. I would try it after the first crew has worked a few weeks without repeat trips.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The planners and buyers may see cuts before our line crews do. My own hours look fairly steady, though an automated order could make the field crew carry office mistakes and lose a paid afternoon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would stay on the repair rota and ask to shadow the first crew using the order tablet. In its first year I would compare five completed jobs with their original parts lists and take repeated mismatches to the supervisor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel watchful and a bit curious. I am willing to learn a proven tool. A good screen should mean fewer drives, not fewer people checking the work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you trust the tablet?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five jobs with correct fittings and no extra depot run would be a start. I would ask the stores worker whether the stock count on the screen matches the shelf.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you raise staffing with a group?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If several crews lost paid time, I would ask two colleagues to bring our lists to a staff meeting. Until then I would give the supervisor a chance to correct a bad order.

say: I would distinguish **2028 schedules** from line robots around 2031.
I would ask a **field crew** to check first robot-made joints.
think: At **48**, capable robots may reduce my physical line hours.
Our **three-month reserve** buys search time, not a long break from wages.
do: Keep paid **repair shifts** in 2029 and ask about field inspection jobs.
Apply for a **posted comparable vacancy** and take paid training only if required.
feel: I feel **anxious** about the near robot date, with some options to explore.
S2.quote: Nearby utilities might have line vacancies, but their crews could also face field robots.
fieldNote: Emeka plans to use the **three-year gap** for paid repairs and a conditional search, not an immediate departure in 2028.
His **inspection test** focuses on real site hours because full AI could absorb report writing first.

steps.text: Keep taking paid line repair shifts through 2029
Apply for a posted field inspection vacancy if pay is comparable
Take paid practical inspection training if the posted vacancy requires it

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say full thinking AI in 2028 can write our schedules, while robots able to do line repairs come around 2031. I would want a field crew to test the first robot joint before the company changes the rota.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 45 for the office change and 48 for the robot. Three months saved would let us look for work, but the mortgage and two school-age children need income beyond those three months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would ask the company whether it has paid field equipment inspection roles that lineworkers can move into. In 2029 I would keep taking repair shifts, apply for a posted inspection vacancy if its pay is similar and take a paid practical course only if the vacancy requires it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about how quickly the field date arrives. Nearby utilities might have line vacancies, but their crews could also face field robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask about an inspection vacancy?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would want to know how many hours are on site checking equipment and how many are writing reports. Full AI could write the reports before robots arrive, so I need the field part to be real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you tell the children anything now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the children I am still going to work tomorrow, and my partner and I will handle the money plan. I would not give them a story about a job loss that has not happened.

say: I would ask for **wet-weather robot checks** before field staffing changes.
I would note **2031 office AI** precedes line robots around 2034.
think: At **51**, I may still need full pay for a mortgage.
A **desk-heavy testing role** could shrink once full AI handles reports.
do: Keep paid **line shifts** in 2032 and watch a trial on paid time.
Apply for a **posted testing role** after checking pay and a colleague's experience.
feel: I feel **less rushed** and interested in a proven field role.
S3.quote: I would want to see a colleague doing the job rather than trusting a brochure.
fieldNote: Emeka requires **colleague proof** of field duties and steady pay before taking a new testing role.
He is open to a **paid short trial** but declines an unpaid term of training without an advertised post.

steps.text: Apply for a posted paid field testing job after a colleague demonstrates it
Take a company-paid training afternoon on the robot trial crew if offered

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say five years is time to measure robot repairs in wet weather and ask what people still do. Full thinking AI arrives by 2031 and field robots around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 48 when AI reaches the office and 51 when robots arrive. Our older child might be leaving school then, but I cannot count on a cleared mortgage or an early retirement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would ask the training supervisor for the criteria of any paid field testing role. In 2032 I would stay on the line rota, watch the robot trial on paid time and apply for a posted testing job if another crew has shown the training works and the pay is steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel less rushed than in the two-year version. I could learn to inspect a robot repair, but I would want to see a colleague doing the job rather than trusting a brochure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the colleague show you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask to watch a robot joint get checked after rain, including the final electrical test. If the tester spends most of the day at a desk, full AI could do too much of that role.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take training before the post opens?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would take a company-paid training afternoon on a trial crew, but I would wait on a longer course until a post was advertised. A short trial is affordable; an unpaid term away from work is not.

say: I would request **yearly crew-hour data** and winter robot rework records.
I would distinguish **2036 office AI** from line robots around 2039.
think: At **56**, grown children do not guarantee a paid mortgage or funded retirement.
My **three-month reserve** can support a transfer, but not years without work.
do: Keep paid **line shifts** in 2037 and review yearly field hours.
Apply for a **posted testing role** if my hours fall and pay is comparable.
feel: I feel **steady now** while I wait for tested robot results.
S4.quote: A robot date on a chart is not by itself a reason to leave a paid job.
fieldNote: Emeka expects **continued paid physical work** over the near term and measures actual field hours before moving.
He keeps the **existing reserve** rather than claiming new savings or assuming retirement at 56.

steps.text: Continue paid line repair shifts through 2037
Apply for a posted field testing role if his repair hours fall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell colleagues that a decade gives crews time to record which robot repairs last through a winter. Full AI changes the office around 2036, and robots able to repair lines arrive around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 53 in 2036 and 56 for the robot date. The children may have grown, but our mortgage might remain, and I do not know whether we could live on retirement money at 56.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would keep field repairs and ask for yearly data on crew hours and robot rework. In 2037 I would stay on paid line shifts, review those figures with my partner and apply for a posted field testing job if my own hours were dropping and its pay was comparable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel steady about the next few years. I can keep earning while the company proves what the robots do, and we have three months saved if a transfer takes time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay extra against the mortgage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep our current payments and reserve for now. I would not call the three months of money we already have new savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you stay on the line?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If real field hours remain and the crew still needs me for repairs, I would stay. A robot date on a chart is not by itself a reason to leave a paid job.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which worries you most, and what would actually help?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because robots could do the field repair around 2031, when my children still need a regular wage at home. A posted inspection job with real site duties, paid practical training and honest robot trial results would help me decide.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask what a field inspection job pays after AI writes its reports. A new title is not a safer job if the company can remove most of its paid hours.

headlineQuote: A new title is not a safer job if the company can remove most of its paid hours.
portrait: Emeka is a **43-year-old lineworker** with an apprenticeship, a partner, two school-age children and a mortgage.
He uses **AI occasionally** after colleagues test it, then checks signed records and physical fittings.
His **three-month reserve**, typical pay and some nearby employers give time to check vacancies.
Across the scenarios he seeks **colleague proof**, paid practical trials and field roles with steady wages.
biggestWorry: The **2028 picture** leaves about three years before robots could take on his physical repair work.
whatWouldHelp: A **posted field job** with real site duties, paid training and honest trial results would help him decide.
